The Generative AI internship in short

In the SkillMe Generative AI internship you build one of 3 projects, such as StudyBuddy: AI Study Assistant & Chatbot, a project where you build a friendly command-line chatbot that helps you revise a subject, then grow it into a remembering, well-behaved study assistant with a UI. In week 1 you get a free LLM API key, make your first working API call from Python, and build a simple terminal chatbot that answers one question at a time. By week 4 you give StudyBuddy a proper chat UI with Streamlit, add basic guardrails so it stays on-topic and safe, and write a small evaluation set to check its answer quality. Each milestone is posted on LinkedIn and checked against that week's checklist before it counts. Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month.

Week by week

What each week of the Generative AI internship covers

Shown for StudyBuddy: AI Study Assistant & Chatbot. The other projects follow the same four-week shape.

  1. Week 1 of 4

    Your First LLM API Call

    Beginner2-3 hours

    Get a free LLM API key, make your first working API call from Python, and build a simple terminal chatbot that answers one question at a time. This week is about the basic mechanics of talking to an LLM safely, before anything fancier.

    What you learn

    • Getting and using a free-tier LLM API key (Google Gemini API or Groq)
    • Keeping secrets out of code with a .env file and python-dotenv
    • Making a basic chat completion request and reading the response
    • Writing a simple loop that takes input and prints a reply

    What you submit

    • A working ask_llm(prompt) function wrapping one provider's API
    • A .env file (untracked) holding the API key, loaded with python-dotenv
    • A terminal chat loop that answers study questions one at a time
    • A README with setup steps that do not expose any real key
    How week 1 is reviewed
    • Running the script and asking a question returns a real, relevant answer from the API
    • The API key never appears anywhere in the committed code or Git history
    • A deliberately broken key or no internet connection shows a friendly error, not a crash
    • Typing quit exits the loop cleanly

    Stretch goal: Let the user pick a subject at startup (e.g. 'DBMS', 'Python') and prepend it to the system instruction so answers stay on-topic.

  2. Week 2 of 4

    Prompt Templates and Conversation Memory

    Beginner+2-3 hours

    Make StudyBuddy actually remember the conversation and respond consistently by introducing prompt templates, a proper system prompt, and a message history list. This is the difference between a one-shot Q&A script and something that feels like a real assistant.

    What you learn

    • Writing a clear, reusable system prompt that sets the assistant's behaviour
    • Building prompt templates with placeholders for reusable question types
    • Keeping a conversation history list and sending it with each request
    • Managing context length by trimming old messages

    What you submit

    • A Conversation class that tracks message history across turns
    • A prompts.py file with a system prompt and at least two prompt templates
    • Working /explain and /quiz commands built on the templates
    • A history-trimming rule that keeps requests from growing forever
    How week 2 is reviewed
    • A follow-up question like 'explain that more simply' gets a relevant answer referencing the previous topic
    • /explain <topic> and /quiz <topic> both produce sensibly formatted, on-topic responses
    • The system prompt is sent exactly once per conversation, not repeated in every message
    • A long chat (15+ turns) keeps working without the request growing unbounded

    Stretch goal: Add a /save command that writes the conversation history to a JSON file and a /load command that resumes it later.

  3. Week 3 of 4

    Answer Questions from Your Own Notes

    Intermediate2-3 hours

    Give StudyBuddy the ability to answer questions using your own study notes instead of only general knowledge, by building a simple retrieval system: chunk your notes, embed them, and find the most relevant pieces for each question. This is a hands-on, simplified introduction to how RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) works.

    What you learn

    • Splitting long text into overlapping chunks
    • Generating embeddings for text with an embeddings API
    • Comparing embeddings with cosine similarity to find relevant chunks
    • Building a prompt that includes retrieved context (a simple RAG pipeline)

    What you submit

    • A chunk_text function that splits notes into overlapping chunks
    • An embedding + caching pipeline for all chunks
    • A retrieve(question) function using cosine similarity
    • A /notes <question> command that answers using retrieved context
    How week 3 is reviewed
    • A question clearly answered in your notes returns a correct, grounded answer
    • A question unrelated to your notes gets an honest 'not covered' response instead of a made-up answer
    • Re-running the app does not re-embed every chunk from scratch (embeddings are cached)
    • retrieve() returns chunks that are genuinely relevant to the question, not random ones

    Stretch goal: Show the source chunk(s) used for each answer underneath the response, so you can see exactly what the model was grounded on.

  4. Week 4 of 4

    Streamlit UI, Evaluation and Guardrails

    Intermediate+2-3 hours

    Give StudyBuddy a proper chat UI with Streamlit, add basic guardrails so it stays on-topic and safe, and write a small evaluation set to check its answer quality. This is the polish that turns a script into a demoable product.

    What you learn

    • Building a chat interface with Streamlit's chat elements and session state
    • Writing simple guardrails: input filtering and instructed refusal behaviour
    • Building a small evaluation set and scoring answers against expected content
    • Documenting a GenAI project, including its known limitations

    What you submit

    • A Streamlit chat UI with session-based history and a notes uploader
    • A basic guardrail that refuses clearly off-topic or unsafe questions
    • An eval_questions.json set and an evaluate.py script with a pass/fail summary
    • A complete README with setup, usage and known limitations, plus a demo video
    How week 4 is reviewed
    • streamlit run app.py opens a chat UI where messages persist across turns in the session
    • Uploading a new notes file makes its content usable in /notes-style answers within the same session
    • At least one deliberately off-topic or unsafe test question is refused politely
    • python evaluate.py runs at least 8 checks and reports how many passed

    Stretch goal: Add a thumbs-up/thumbs-down button on each answer in the UI and log the feedback to a file for later review.

Is it for you?

Who the Generative AI internship is for, and what you leave with

This internship fits you if

  • You know the basics of LLM APIs, Prompting and RAG and want a real project to show for it, not more tutorials.
  • You can start at beginner level. Week 1: Get a free LLM API key, make your first working API call from Python, and build a simple terminal chatbot that answers one question at a time.
  • You want to reach intermediate+ level in four weeks. Week 4: Give StudyBuddy a proper chat UI with Streamlit, add basic guardrails so it stays on-topic and safe, and write a small evaluation set to check its answer quality.
  • You can give it about 2-3 hours a week around college or a job, from any country.

Generative AI internship: questions and answers

What will I build in the Generative AI internship?

You are assigned one of 3 projects: StudyBuddy: AI Study Assistant & Chatbot, DocuMind: Document Q&A Tool with Retrieval or ContentForge: Prompt-Powered Content Generator. Each is a single project built up over four weekly milestones, so each week adds to the last.

What skills will I learn in the Generative AI internship?

The Generative AI internship works with LLM APIs, Prompting and RAG. Week 1: getting and using a free-tier LLM API key (Google Gemini API or Groq); keeping secrets out of code with a .env file and python-dotenv. Week 2: writing a clear, reusable system prompt that sets the assistant's behaviour; building prompt templates with placeholders for reusable question types. Week 3: splitting long text into overlapping chunks; generating embeddings for text with an embeddings API. Week 4: building a chat interface with Streamlit's chat elements and session state; writing simple guardrails: input filtering and instructed refusal behaviour.

Do I need experience to apply for the Generative AI internship?

You need the basics of LLM APIs, Prompting and RAG, not prior internship experience. Week 1 starts at beginner level, where you get a free LLM API key, make your first working API call from Python, and build a simple terminal chatbot that answers one question at a time. Week 4 reaches intermediate+ level. A short screening quiz (8 questions, about 5 minutes) checks you are ready to start.

How is each Generative AI milestone reviewed?

Every week has a checklist, and a milestone is approved only when it meets all of it. For week 1 of StudyBuddy: AI Study Assistant & Chatbot, that means: running the script and asking a question returns a real, relevant answer from the API; the API key never appears anywhere in the committed code or Git history; a deliberately broken key or no internet connection shows a friendly error, not a crash; typing quit exits the loop cleanly. Reviewers include engineers who work at Walmart, Google and LinkedIn, and work that misses the bar comes back with notes.

What can I put on my resume after the Generative AI internship?

Each approved milestone gives you a line you can back up with a public LinkedIn post: Made my first LLM API call from Python using a free-tier provider; Built a terminal study chatbot with safe API key handling via .env; Learned to handle network and API errors gracefully instead of crashing; Added conversation memory to my AI study assistant using a message history list; Designed a system prompt and reusable prompt templates for explain and quiz modes; Learned to manage context length by trimming old messages safely; Built a simple retrieval pipeline that lets my AI assistant answer from my own notes; Implemented text chunking and embeddings with cosine similarity by hand; Learned the core idea behind RAG by grounding LLM answers in retrieved context; Built a full Streamlit chat UI for my AI study assistant with persistent session history; Added guardrails so the assistant refuses off-topic or unsafe questions; Wrote an evaluation script to measure answer quality against expected keywords.

What are the other projects in the Generative AI internship?

DocuMind: Document Q&A Tool with Retrieval: Build a tool that lets you ask questions about your own PDFs and text files and get answers grounded in their actual content. ContentForge: Prompt-Powered Content Generator: Build a tool that generates social posts, captions and blog outlines from a topic, then turn it into a structured, controllable content pipeline. Every project follows the same four-week shape, with one reviewed milestone a week.

Is the Generative AI internship paid? Is there a stipend?

Top performers earn a stipend of up to $100 a month. It is performance-based: 8–10 interns are picked each month from those who complete the internship and hold an issued certificate. It is not paid to every intern.

How much time does it take?

4 weeks, one milestone a week, each planned for about 2-3 hours. It is fully remote and open worldwide, so you work around college or a job.
